content: The surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula involves specific considerations and methodologies. The search strategy for relevant literature included terms such as vaginal fistula, vesicovaginal, urinary, obstetric, female genital, and fistula, applied to both titles and abstracts. This yielded 616 results. A secondary search focused on catheterization, using terms like catheter, catheter care, and cannulation, which resulted in 594 entries. Combining these two searches produced 54 relevant studies. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations regarding the duration of bladder catheterization following the surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula. These recommendations are based on a thorough review of evidence, including the quality of the data, patient values and preferences, the balance of benefits and harms, cost/resource implications, and considerations of equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included several experts and contributors. Dr. Dolores Nembunzu, a content expert and end-user, served as an investigator in the Barone 2015 trial. Although she was accepted as a GDG member, she did not have voting rights. Similarly, Dr. Muleta and Dr. Arrowsmith were also members without voting rights. Their conflicts of interest were deemed not significant enough to affect their participation in the group. Dr. Mark Barone, a content expert and implementer, was the principal investigator of the Barone 2015 trial. He did not have voting rights and did not participate in discussions regarding the final recommendations. Dr. Asseefa Mekonnen, a consumer representative, declared no conflicts of interest. Dr. Maria Regina Torloni and Ms. Ewelina Rogozinska, both methodologists, also declared no conflicts of interest and did not have voting rights. The WHO's recommendations on bladder catheterization duration after surgical repair of simple obstetric urinary fistula are supported by an evidence-to-decision framework. This framework evaluates the quality of evidence, the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, resource implications, and issues of equity, acceptability, and feasibility. These factors collectively inform the strength and direction of the recommendations.
